Creative Engineering Design

About the Course

Creative Engineering Design is a project-based course in which first-year students in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Seoul National University work in teams to design and build their own robots. First introduced in 1993 by the late Professor Chong Nam Chu, it has continued for more than 30 years and has become a signature engineering course at the SNU College of Engineering. Students conceive robots that carry out a given mission, then build and test them within limited conditions, developing creativity, teamwork and engineering problem-solving skills along the way. The course content has changed steadily to reflect advances in technology, and since 2024 it has used remote-control devices as a foundation for teaching AI robot architecture.

Course Objectives and Description

This course aims to develop a basic sense of design and fabrication, as well as creativity, through hands-on design and fabrication of a variety of given targets. Intended for first-year students who have not yet formed a clear concept of engineering, it has students build products themselves from specified materials and compete with them, so that they can experience the meaning of engineering with genuine interest. The products take many forms, such as mechanisms and structures, that together reflect the characteristics of various engineering fields. The course is structured so that students with little experience in coding or hardware can learn step by step from the introductory stage.

Building on Internet of Things (IoT) technology, which is widely used across industrial devices and home appliances including automobiles, robots and smartphones, students use microcontrollers (Arduino, 32-bit MCUs, etc.) to understand the basic structure of an MCU, collect data through sensors for temperature, humidity, light, sound, motion and images, and learn the principles of connecting and controlling output devices such as displays and motors. They then connect objects through wired and wireless communication and implement on-device AI (TinyML), which learns and infers directly on the device. In this way, they complete the entire process from sensing to reasoning and action as a single integrated system, extending to Physical AI—artificial intelligence that perceives, reasons about and acts upon the real world on its own. By combining theory with hands-on practice, the course connects with other engineering design courses, from the fundamentals through to prototype development.

The course consists of two hours of lecture and two hours of lab each week. During the first six weeks, lectures on basic design principles, kinematics and fabrication methods are combined with robot programming practice and fabrication. In week 7, the purpose and rules of the robots that students will design and build are announced, and in week 12 the main competition is held with the robots each team has freely designed and built within the given rules, using the materials and tools provided.

Curriculum

Machine Learning for Mechanical Engineering
Computer-aided design and software fundamentals
Creative Engineering Design
Robot hardware, motor control, basic circuits and building a working robot

SNU Robocon

The course culminates in Robocon, a team competition in which every student competes with the robot they built in class. The winning team goes on to represent Korea at an international Robocon competition.

Student Reviews

Reflections from teams that took part in Robocon.

Our TA told us later, “What you did is the textbook approach, but in practice people rarely do it.” When you just talk, there are plenty of good ideas. But until you build them, you can’t know whether they work. Whenever we had an idea, we built a simple version and tested it, and we built our final robot only from the ideas that proved to work. We thought every team did that, but it turned out they didn’t. When we won, I thought of everything we had been through and couldn’t hold back my tears.

2022 · 30th Robocon · Team Zero · Winner

With a week left, we tore down both of our robots, even though they had been rated well, and started over. Our TA asked if we were crazy, but we were determined to finish first, so we chose a week of all-nighters. In the evaluation rounds you only need to perform well on your own, but at Robocon robots face off against each other, so we thought we had to rebuild a robot that wins. The strategy worked. We missed the title amid real-world variables, but even if we could turn back time, we couldn’t have done better. We gave it everything.

2022 · 30th Robocon · Team Emergency Rescue · Runner-up

Determined to win the Robocon game, we stuck together all semester and lived with the rulebook. Because we were always thinking about winning, we had more ideas than we could use. We built and tested many versions over and over, and made it to the semifinals. I came to this department out of respect for mechanical engineering, which built aircraft carriers and went to the moon before the internet existed. After Robocon, though, I realized how important management and strategy are, so I’ve applied for a double major in a related field.

2022 · 30th Robocon · Team-3 · Semifinalist · Engineering Award

I spent a lot of time on Creative Engineering Design. But spending a lot of time doesn’t mean things go as planned. Coming up with ideas, building all night, failing… meeting, rebuilding… and it was so much fun! I’ll tell younger students to take the course in their first year. It’s a shortcut to discovering your identity as a mechanical engineer, and if you’ve chosen the wrong department, you’ll find that out through the course too.

2022 · 30th Robocon · Team Triple S (SS.S) · Semifinalist · Creativity Award

When we formed the team, we thought the title was ours. We’re all high school friends, and though our dreams differ, we came together because we all love physics. We believed we had built the best robot in physical terms, and our first and second evaluation results were good. Not thinking much about how to beat the other robots is what stopped us in the quarterfinals. My dream is to become a CEO, and the course felt a lot like starting a company, so I learned a great deal.

2022 · 30th Robocon · Team MEshiah · Quarterfinalist

When a preliminary match went wrong, we were offered a rematch, but we believed an unbreakable spirit mattered more, so we proudly chose to bow out. Our team is a group of true believers who love physics and math and love machines that move. No regrets. Right after withdrawing, we went straight to the gym to rebuild the stamina we had lost.

2022 · 30th Robocon · Team ABCÉD · Round of 16
